column3: Closely parallels gardens of palms and grapes with springs caused to flow within them.

The same-surah parable joins rain-fed vegetation and its rapid ruin to the transience beneath the garden owner's confidence.
It explicitly identifies wealth and children as worldly adornment, the value system exposed by the owner's boast.
A garden of palms and grapes with rivers and all fruit, then threatened with ruin, closely anticipates the focus parable's productive wealth and loss.
Rain produces gardens, palms, grapes, and fruit, providing a close creation-and-yield counterpart.
Rain revives dead land and brings forth every fruit, giving the wider divine pattern behind fertile yield.
Good land yields vegetation by its Lord's permission, making divine authorization of productivity explicit.
Water-grown vegetation that flourishes and is suddenly reduced closely parallels worldly abundance's instability.
Rivers, paired fruits, and gardens of grapes provide a close landscape counterpart to the focus scene.
Rain bringing fruits and rivers under divine disposal supplies the wider provision-and-water frame.
Rain for drinking and pasture establishes water as God's provision for cultivated life.
Water causing crops, olives, palms, grapes, and other fruits to grow closely expands the focus's agricultural imagery.
Water sent from the sky brings varied vegetation, a broader account of the productive order in the gardens.
Rain turning the earth green provides a concise fertility counterpart.
Measured water sent down and settled in the earth clarifies the controlled water source underlying garden fertility.
That water brings gardens of palms and grapes with abundant fruits and food, making it a near parallel.
Gardens and springs are named together as bestowed abundance.
Gardens and springs in the Thamud address offer another scene of granted agricultural security.
Crops and palm trees with delicate fruit extend the abundance imagery associated with the focus gardens.
Heaven-sent water produces splendid gardens whose trees people cannot cause to grow, directly stressing divine agency.
Water driven to barren land brings crops consumed by people and livestock, a strong provision-and-irrigation parallel.
The two gardens on right and left, with a command to eat God's provision, is the immediate positive counterpart to their later replacement.
Dead earth revived to produce grain frames garden fruit as a sign of divinely given sustenance.
Eating the gardens' fruit and what divine power produced emphasizes provision rather than human self-sufficiency.
Rain channeled as springs brings diverse crops that later wither, closely pairing water-fed abundance with transience.
Measured rain brings a revived land and gardens, reinforcing deliberate divine provision.
Blessed rain brings gardens and harvest grain, a close account of productive abundance from above.
The same rain provides sustenance for servants, clarifying the provisioning purpose of fertile growth.
The rain-fed growth that delights then dries out gives a strong worldly-transience analogy to the garden owner's false security.
The prospect of water sinking away directly echoes the threatened loss of accessible garden water in 18:41.
Divine bounty is expressed as wealth, children, gardens, and rivers, closely linking the assets central to the parable.
Gardens and grapevines provide a concise reward-side counterpart to the focus's grape gardens.
Poured water begins the explicit sequence that yields the food and gardens later named in the passage.
Grapes are named among the produce supplied through the water-and-earth sequence.
Gardens are named among the provisions produced for human and livestock use.
A flowing spring within a high garden offers a paradisal water-and-garden counterpart.
The same surah calls earthly beauty an adornment and a test, directly framing the owner's gardens and wealth.
The same surah warns that the adorned earth can become barren dust, anticipating the garden's threatened collapse.
Faith and reverence opening blessings from heaven and earth provide a moral counterpoint to abundance misread through association.
Turning back to the Lord is joined to abundant rain and increased strength, linking restored obedience to provision.
Pure water sent from the sky supplies the larger mercy-and-provision source behind fertility.
Two gushing springs in the two gardens make an especially close water-system counterpart.
Fruit, palms, and pomegranates in the two gardens closely parallel the focus's orchard abundance.
The question about cultivated crops shifts attention from human planting to the divine power behind yield.
The possibility that crops become debris provides a loss-of-yield contrast to the focus's initial completeness.
